Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, hypervigilance to sudden movements by other people is a poor thematic fit. It suggests an interpersonal/assault-type threat rather than danger linked to environmental cues or disaster reminders.

issues.item: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: Avoiding unfamiliar places because danger cannot be assessed is more consistent with persistent fear of human threat or assault in public settings than with a natural-disaster index trauma. In this profile there are no corresponding disaster-specific trigger or memory items that would make this threat pattern cohere.

issues.item: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: Self-blame based on one's character is a weak fit for a natural-disaster trauma. Some survivor guilt or responsibility appraisals can occur, but this item implies dispositional blame for an uncontrollable event, which is clinically harder to reconcile here, especially without complementary appraisal content about responsibility or preventability.

issues.item: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these two items are hard to reconcile as a coherent pair for the same trauma memory. 'Photographic Recall' implies a vivid, detailed, visually accessible memory that feels directly available, whereas 'Memory Feels Alien' suggests marked detachment/disownership of the memory. These can both occur in PTSD, but endorsed together as defining memory qualities for the same event is clinically tense and would likely prompt questioning of coherence. The rest of the profile is broadly consistent with severe post-disaster PTSD, and the Negative Appraisals ↔ Threat/Memory pattern is plausible.

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: The threat profile is partly coherent for severe PTSD after a natural disaster (hypervigilance to sounds, sleep disturbance), but 'avoiding unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger' fits a generalized danger/assault-style threat schema more than a natural-disaster trauma pattern. For this trauma type, threat is more plausibly cued by weather, environmental instability, or disaster reminders. This item is not impossible, but it is the least coherent with the specified trauma context and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Uncontrolled Access' and 'Fragmented Pieces' suggest intrusive, poorly elaborated trauma memory, which aligns with the formulation. By contrast, 'Memory Feels Alien' implies marked depersonalization/dissociative detachment from the memory. That can occur clinically, but paired with the very high PCL-5 and the rest of the profile it introduces a qualitatively different dissociative presentation that is not supported elsewhere in Threat or Negative Appraisals, making this memory item the least internally coherent in the set.

issues.item: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
issues.explanation: This memory item implies a strong trigger-linked reactivation process, but the formulation explicitly marks Triggers → Memory as inactive. The rest of the profile contains no Triggers items, and the formulation centers the case on Negative Appraisals ↔ Threat/Memory links rather than environmental cue-driven retrieval. For this patient, that item conflicts with the specified formulation structure more than the other selected items do.

vignette:
When Ty arrived in the United States years ago from Southeast Asia, she built a life that felt steady and ordinary. At 52, she is married, works long shifts at a fast-food restaurant, and had come to value routine, especially the sense that if she worked hard and kept going, life could be managed. That assumption was badly shaken during the natural disaster she now describes only in broken fragments. When she tries to speak about it, the account does not come out as a single story. Instead, it arrives in jagged pieces: the sudden noise, the sense of the world turning violent without warning, darkness, water and debris where familiar surroundings had been, and the terrifying certainty in those moments that there was nowhere safe to go. Even in session, when she starts to approach the memory, she becomes visibly overwhelmed and has to stop, pressing her lips together and looking down as if to hold herself together. She says the memory does not stay where she puts it. It forces itself into her mind when she is washing dishes, riding home from work, or trying to lie quietly in bed.

In the weeks after the disaster, Ty found that nighttime changed first. Daylight felt somewhat more manageable because she could see what was around her, but after dark she no longer felt she could truly relax. She began checking doors and windows repeatedly before bed, then lying awake listening for anything out of place. Sleep became difficult both at the start of the night and after she finally drifted off. She would wake abruptly and remain alert for long stretches, straining to hear whether some new danger was approaching. What frightened her most was the feeling that bad things did not announce themselves until it was too late. Night came to feel like the hour when she was least protected.

Over the following months, sounds became especially potent. At the restaurant where she works, unexpected loud noises are unavoidable: the crash of a metal tray, the alarm of a timer, someone dropping a stack of frozen goods in the back, the sharp hiss and clatter from the kitchen during a busy rush. Coworkers might glance up and keep moving, but Ty feels her whole body react before she can think. She goes instantly on alert, scanning, her heart pounding, as if the next second might bring catastrophe. She tries not to show it, embarrassed by how strongly she reacts, but she has begun positioning herself away from the noisier stations when she can. On especially hectic shifts she finds herself distracted, braced, and exhausted by the effort of getting through the day. At home, a slammed car door outside or an unexpected thud in the apartment building can make her freeze and listen, fully awake again.

Her own understanding of what has happened to her is bleak and painful. She has come to believe that something in her emotional life has been permanently damaged. She tells herself that she will never feel normal emotions again, and there is a flatness to the way she says this, as if joy, ease, and ordinary comfort now belong to other people. At times she sits with her husband and knows she is supposed to feel close, grateful, or safe, but instead feels distant from herself and from him. She does not describe conflict so much as disconnection. She also carries a growing sense that she no longer belongs anywhere. The life she made in America feels unfamiliar, but the person she was before the disaster also feels unreachable. At work she smiles at customers and follows the script of the shift, yet privately feels set apart, as though she is only acting like someone who fits in.

Running through all of this is a conviction of helplessness. Ty is certain she cannot stop bad things from happening to her. She does not say this dramatically; she says it as if it has been proven. That belief appears in small decisions as much as large ones. She avoids talking in detail about the disaster because once the memory begins, it comes in disconnected pieces and the emotion surges so strongly that she feels she might lose control. She avoids certain conversations, certain television images, and lingers at work after closing if it means getting home before it is fully dark. These habits have narrowed her world. She is tired, less present with her husband, and increasingly worn down by every day requiring vigilance.

What finally brought Ty to seek help was not one new event but the accumulation of nights without rest and the realization that she was organizing her life around noise, darkness, and the effort not to remember. She said she could no longer keep pretending she was fine during her shifts while feeling internally on edge all the time. At the same time, she was frightened that speaking about the disaster would make the memories come back too strongly to bear. More than anything, she wants some way to live without feeling under threat after every sound and every nightfall, though she is not yet sure whether that is still possible for her.
